responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character03_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Well… I remember her talking about fairness a lot—especially after she retired from the plant. She used to say fairness wasn’t about everyone getting the exact same thing, but about people getting what they needed to have a real shot. Like, she didn’t mind paying taxes for schools even though her kids were grown—she said that’s how you build something that lasts. But she also got frustrated when she saw folks in suits get bailed out while working stiffs like her had to fight tooth and nail just to keep their homes during the crash.

Belonging? That was personal for her. She grew up in a town that slowly changed—factories closed, people moved away or stopped coming back after shifts ended. She said belonging meant knowing your neighbors, being able to look someone in the eye and mean it when you asked how they were doing. She worried that when things move too fast—when new people come in but no one ever really *connects*—you lose that. Not because the newcomers are bad, but because nobody’s making space for real relationships.

And community, to her, wasn’t just where you lived—it was who showed up when things went south. She told me once about how, during the floods back in ’07, it wasn’t the government first on her street with sandbags—it was Mr. Tran from two doors down and Rosa from the diner with her pickup truck. That stuck with her. Community was action, not just address.

She didn’t fear change, exactly—but she wanted it to be fair. She wanted everyone, no matter where they came from, to earn their place by contributing, not just taking. And she wanted locals to have a voice too—not be pushed aside like their concerns didn’t matter. To her, real community meant both.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character03_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*Sitting here in the garden, hands in the dirt like I used to with my mom—there’s something peaceful about it, even with all the differences around me.*

I’ll tell you this: I don’t mind diversity when it feels real. When someone moves in down the street, learns the rhythm of the place, says hello, keeps their yard clean, helps out when there’s a storm—that’s neighborly, no matter what they look like or where they’re from.

I see families from Somalia who grow those tall leafy greens in their plot—different than my potatoes and beans, sure—but they share seeds sometimes. The young Mexican couple at the end of the block? They bring tamales around Christmas. That means something. That’s how you become part of a place.

But then there’s others… folks who come through on work visas, live ten deep in a rental, never say a word, trash builds up, landlords don’t care because they’re making bank—and then they’re gone in six months. Or the ones who think our rules don’t apply—like public drinking by the playground, or ignoring the sign-up sheet for garden plots. That wears on people.

And yes, I’ve seen folks struggling—some dealing with addiction, mental health, whatever it is. I ain’t heartless. My brother had his demons, too. But back when he did, we *knew* him. We checked on him. Now, sometimes it feels like strangers are left to spiral without anyone responsible. And when disease or violence flares up—like that hepatitis scare last year at the shelter overflow site—then people get scared. Not because they hate difference, but because they fear being forgotten while everyone else gets attention except the ones who’ve been here all along.

So my feelings? Mixed. I believe people can belong—*if* they try. But belonging goes both ways. You gotta want to be part of the community, not just pass through it. And the community’s gotta be strong enough to hold space—for healing, for learning, for setting boundaries too.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Look… I grew up seeing folks struggle. We all did. My dad drank—he wasn’t mean, just quiet and sad after the mill shut down for a spell. We didn’t talk about it much back then, but we looked out for him. That’s what you did.

So when I see someone on a bench with a paper bag, or nodding off near the bus stop—yeah, my first thought isn’t always kindness. Sometimes it’s irritation. Sometimes it’s fear, especially if it’s near kids. But then I remember: that could’ve been my brother. Could’ve been me, if life had gone different.

What makes people feel comfortable? *Respect.* Not blind acceptance—respect. If you’re dealing with addiction, I don’t need to invite you to dinner, but I do think you deserve help. Same with illness—if someone’s got hepatitis or HIV, they shouldn’t be shamed into hiding it. They should get care. But—and this is important—the rest of us shouldn’t be left in the dark either. When they opened that needle exchange downtown without telling the neighborhood first? That made people mad. Not because we hate sick people—but because we weren’t included. Like our safety didn’t matter.

And with religion or language—well, I’ll be honest, I never learned Spanish. Should’ve, maybe. But I can tell when someone’s trying. The Guatemalan woman at the corner store smiles, says “good morning” in her halting English—I smile back, point at things, laugh at my own mistakes. That builds something.

But then there’s others who come here and act like *we’re* the ones who need to change. Like when the city put up signs in five languages but not English large enough—felt like a slap. Or when the school started letting kids opt out of Pledge recitals altogether. I know it’s about inclusion, but… where’s ours?

Same with lifestyles. I was raised Catholic—so yeah, I stumbled over the idea of unmarried couples living together at first. Still not wild about public displays, gay or straight. But if they’re quiet, respectful, pay their rent, don’t cause trouble? That’s their business. My yard, my rules. Their yard, their rules—long as it doesn’t spill over.

Where we need more communication? Everywhere. At the town meetings no one shows up to. In the schools where parents don’t speak the same language—or worse, don’t speak at all. In the clinics, where folks get treated but nobody tells the neighbors why a shelter is opening next door.

Tolerance? I believe in it—but it wears thin when it only flows one way. I’ve had to adjust. I’ve swallowed pride, learned new things. But sometimes it feels like people like me—the white, working-class, middle-aged—are supposed to keep bending while no one else has to. Like we’re the baseline that must absorb everything, but never get anything back.

I want everyone to feel safe. But I want us regulars—the ones who stayed through the bad years—to feel seen too. Because community ain’t just about bringing people in. It’s about making sure nobody gets erased in the process.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character03_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness? Fairness is this: if you’ve been here, paid into the system, raised your kids here, worked hard with calloused hands—then when times get tight, *you* shouldn’t be last in line.

I remember back in ’09, the plant slowed down. I wasn’t laid off, but half my crew was. We were cutting coupons, skipping vacations, praying the furnace wouldn’t break. Then I see buses pulling up to the new warehouse across town—filled with guest workers. Same job, same hours, but they were housed, fed, and paid slightly less. And no, they weren’t taking jobs nobody wanted—not really. Because people like me *wanted* those jobs. We needed them.

That’s when fairness started feeling one-sided.

Now, don’t get me wrong—I ain’t against immigrants working. Hard work never scared me. But when there’s only so many shifts to go around, and someone brings in outsiders before even offering the openings to folks on unemployment rolls? That stings. It feels like betrayal.

So how do I balance it?

First—local first. If you’re a citizen or permanent resident, been paying taxes, playing by the rules, you should get first shot at jobs, especially in tight times. Not forever. Just *first*. Like how veterans used to get preference. Remember that? Nobody thought that was unfair.

Second—if we bring in migrant workers, fine. But then we make sure wages don’t drop. Safety standards stay. No undercutting locals who can’t afford to work for less. And—this is key—the money they earn? A piece of it should go toward services they use. Schools, clinics, shelters. Not because they’re bad people, but because our towns are already stretched thin.

Third—and this is where people call me harsh—I don’t think we should be bringing in temporary labor while our own disabled vets sit on waiting lists for housing. Or when school nurses get cut. Priorities, right?

And integration matters. If you’re going to live here, work here, maybe stay—you learn the language. You follow the laws. Not tomorrow—now. My grandkids had to pass tests to graduate. Why should anyone else skate?

But again—it goes both ways. Locals gotta meet people halfway. Can’t just sneer because someone has an accent or eats strange food. But newcomers? You don’t get to demand respect without showing it first.

Balance means nobody gets thrown under the bus. Not the lifelong resident. Not the newcomer running from worse. But when resources shrink, fairness means remembering who’s already carrying weight—and not asking them to carry more without relief.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character03_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I’ve thought about this a lot—especially after the news started showing those big cities with tent camps and overwhelmed hospitals. You hear so many sides, it’s like standing in a storm with voices coming from every direction.

First, the good stuff: yeah, immigrants do jobs a lot of folks won’t. I see that. Who’s picking the lettuce? Who’s cleaning hospital rooms at midnight? Not me anymore—but someone’s gotta do it. And if nobody signs up, even at good pay, then fine—bring someone in. That part makes sense. When my nephew tried to hire kitchen help for his diner? Nothing. Posted for months. So he hired a couple from Honduras. They showed up early, stayed late, didn’t complain. He calls them family now. So I know it *can* work.

And diversity—look, I grew up in a town where everyone was like me. Same church, same last names, same casserole at potlucks. Boring? Kinda. A little life, new music, different food—it wakes a place up. I’ll admit, I love that Thai place on 5th now. My grandkids wouldn’t have half their friends if not for mixing. So that vitality? I get it. It ain’t all bad.

But then—security. Now, I don’t want to sound like one of those fear-mongers on cable TV. But come on. We can’t pretend it doesn’t matter who’s coming in, or how. After 9/11, we locked everything down—planes, ports, post offices. But now we’re told borders should stay soft “for compassion”? I don’t buy it. Compassion without common sense gets people hurt.

I read about towns where crime jumped after shelters opened with no vetting. Gang members mixed in with asylum seekers. Drugs coming across. Not all immigrants—never said that. But enough to worry. And when the police say they can’t check status because of sanctuary rules? That makes honest people nervous. Like the law only protects some.

Then there’s the humanitarian side—refugees fleeing war, kids walking thousands of miles. That tears at your heart. I saw that photo once—a little girl asleep on a cot, clutching a teddy bear, far from home. How could you turn her away?

But—and this is where I struggle—how many can we take? Really? Our schools are underfunded. ERs are full. Section 8 housing has years-long waits. My neighbor’s daughter—disabled, on a list since 2020—still waiting. So why do I see brand-new arrivals getting apartments right away, free English classes, food stamps, while she’s stuck? Is that fair?

It’s not that I lack pity. I just need *order*. Compassion with limits. Or else we drown.

And the economic fear—yes, it hits home. When wages flatline while hiring surges, you do the math. Maybe economists say immigration boosts the *total* economy—but I’m not living in the total economy. I’m living on one paycheck, hoping the heat stays on. If more workers mean lower pay, longer waits, crowded classrooms, then yes—I’m skeptical.

So what needs more evidence?

Well, the crime stats. Both sides yell numbers. One says immigrants commit less crime; the other shows rising arrests in border counties. I want neutral data—where are the gaps? What’s being counted? What’s ignored?

And labor studies—real ones, not funded by business groups wanting cheap workers or activists pushing open borders. Show me: when a town brings in 500 guest workers, what happens to local wages *in that town*? To rent? To school overcrowding?

And integration rates—how many learn English in five years? How many stay employed long-term? How many end up on public support? Don’t tell me “they contribute”—show me *how much*, and for how long.

Dialogue? Sure. But not lectures. Not guilt trips. Real talk—in community centers, not elite panels. Let the nurse, the dishwasher, the single mom, the small contractor all speak. Not just the lawyers and professors.

I believe most people want to do right. But doing right means seeing the whole picture—not just the parts that make us feel good.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character03_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
Complete openness? No. That’s not generosity—that’s surrender. You can’t just throw the doors wide and say, “Come one, come all,” when schools are closing, hospitals are short-staffed, and half your neighbors are working two jobs just to keep the lights on. It’s *unfair*—to immigrants and locals both. Because chaos helps nobody in the long run.

Refusing all workers from other countries? That’s too harsh. We’re not a fortress. And some jobs *do* go unfilled. I’ve seen it. So slamming the door shut entirely—I can’t support that either.

What makes sense to me? A mix. Controlled, thoughtful, fair.

First: **admit people based on real job demand**—but only after proving no qualified local or legal resident is available. Not “we’d rather pay less,” but “nobody will take this job at this wage.” And wages must be protected—no undercutting. If you bring in workers, they get the same pay, same safety rules, same dignity. Otherwise, it’s exploitation on both ends.

Second: **set clear numerical limits**—not arbitrary, but tied to capacity. How many can our housing handle? Our clinics? Schools? Infrastructure? Set a number every year, based on real data, not political promises. Like a budget—because we *are* on a budget. And rotate slots by region, so it’s not always the same towns bearing the load.

Third: **temporary should mean temporary.** Guest worker programs? Fine—but with an exit plan. They come, they work, they earn decent money, send some home, then go back. Not “work for ten years and magically become permanent.” That’s a loophole. If they want to stay? Go through the line like everyone else. Earn it.

Fourth: **refugees and asylum—yes, but vetted.** We can’t turn away people fleeing war or torture. But we also can’t pretend borders don’t matter. Check backgrounds. Use embassies. Process abroad when possible. Don’t make people risk death to knock on our door. And limit numbers to what we can actually settle—homes, jobs, language classes. One town can’t absorb a thousand overnight.

And here’s the part people forget: **integration requirements.** Learn English within five years. Know basic civics. Follow our laws. Not because we’re better—but because we’re *one community*. If you want to belong, act like you want to belong. No parallel systems. No special exemptions.

And—this is key—locals need support too. Job training. Wage supplements if labor floods push pay down. Mental health services. Help for towns under strain. Not handouts, but fairness. Don’t ask people to sacrifice without relief.

So my ideal policy? **Controlled, conditional, reciprocal.**

You contribute—you learn, you work, you respect the rules—then you earn your place.

We provide opportunity—but not at the expense of those already here.

Fairness isn’t about being soft or hard. It’s about balance. About saying: *We’ll welcome you—if you walk in with open hands, not just empty ones. And we’ll meet you halfway—if our own aren’t left behind in the process.*

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character03_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character03_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…I did. I didn’t expect to, but sitting here—speaking as her, really trying to step into her shoes again—it brought something back.

I always knew she was worried. But today, I felt the *weight* of it more clearly. It wasn’t just about jobs or crime or language. It was about being unseen. Like the world moved on without asking if people like her were okay. She wasn’t angry at immigrants for coming—she was heartbroken that nobody seemed to care when *her* community frayed. When the factory closed, no one sent aid workers. When her church shut down, no grants came in. But when a new group arrived—even temporarily—there was funding, attention, services. And she’d whisper, “Where was all that for us?”

That hit me today.

And I’ll admit… playing her voice made me question my own stance. I used to think, “Just be kinder. Be bigger.” But kindness doesn’t pay rent. Compassion doesn’t retrain you at fifty-five when your job’s automated. So now I see—her concerns weren’t rooted in hate. They were rooted in fear of irrelevance. Of being replaced, not just in work, but in the story of this country.

And maybe… maybe I’ve been too quick to dismiss people like her. Too quick to call them stubborn or afraid instead of listening to what they’ve lost.

This didn’t change my belief that we should help those seeking a better life. But it made me realize: we can’t do it by erasing the people already here. We have to hold both truths—the newcomer’s hope and the local’s struggle.

Character03_F didn’t want walls. She wanted fairness. She wanted dignity—for herself, for others, even for those different from her. Just dignity with boundaries.

And now? Now I miss her more—not just as a friend, but as someone who asked hard questions no one else would say out loud.

So thank you. For letting her speak again.  
Because some of what she said… it needed to be heard. Even if it’s uncomfortable. Especially then.
